drapeaux.note: The phrase "the whole proceeding is a mask" is quoted from the official English text of Moore v. Dempsey, 261 U.S. 86 (1923), checked against https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/261/86 (the passage reads "But if the case is that the whole proceeding is a mask—that counsel, jury and judge were swept to the fatal end..."). The French entry places it in quotation marks in English already.

titre: Moore v. Dempsey: forty-five minutes of trial, and the mask
accroche: Arkansas, 1919: five Black men are sentenced to death after a trial lasting forty-five minutes. In 1923, Holmes writes that a trial can be nothing but a mask.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 30, 1919, in Phillips County, Arkansas, Black people gathered in a church are fired on by white men. A white man is killed in the fighting, and Black people are then hunted down and shot across the region. On October 1, another white man, Clinton Lee, is killed. Five Black men are charged with his murder.

A warning is in order about what follows. The account you are about to read is not that of an investigation: it is the one the condemned men set out in their petition. Justice Holmes says so himself: the Court does not vouch for it, it takes it as true because the State answered with a mere procedural objection, without contesting it.

## A forty-five-minute trial

According to the petition, a mob goes to the jail to lynch the accused. Federal soldiers keep it out, and prominent citizens, members of a committee appointed by the governor, calm it by promising that the law will take its course, meaning that the guilty will be executed in due form. Black witnesses are said to have been whipped and tortured until they said what was expected of them, among them those whose testimony was used to convict the accused.

The five men appear on November 3 before an all-white jury, Black people being systematically excluded from juries. Their court-appointed lawyer asks for no postponement, no change of venue, no separate trials, challenges no juror, has had no prior consultation with them, calls no witness and does not let them speak. The trial lasts about forty-five minutes. The jury deliberates for less than five minutes and finds all five men guilty of first-degree murder. They are sentenced to death.

## The mask

The Arkansas Supreme Court upholds the convictions. A federal court in turn rejects the condemned men's application. Since *Frank v. Mangum* (1915), the U.S. Supreme Court has accepted that a trial dominated by a mob violates due process, but it leaves it to the States to correct that defect themselves.

On February 19, 1923, Holmes writes for the Court: a mere error of law cannot be corrected this way, but if "the whole proceeding is a mask," if the lawyer, the jury and the judge were swept along by a wave of public passion, and the State courts did not make it right, then the Court can secure the condemned men's rights. It does not rule on their guilt. It sends the case back to the federal judge, who must determine whether the alleged facts are true.

## The shift

Justice McReynolds, dissenting, sees a risk: the federal route opened to every convict of a State, at the expense of swift punishment. The ruling has another effect: a trial that has every outward form (a lawyer, a jury, a judge, a verdict) does not protect what the form is supposed to protect. According to Wikipedia, freedom does not come in 1923: the governor commutes the sentences on November 11, 1925, and the men are released several months later. What is left of a right that takes six years to be applied?

repere.texte: On February 19, 1923, in Moore v. Dempsey, the U.S. Supreme Court (opinion of Justice Holmes) takes as true that the trial of five Black men sentenced to death in Arkansas lasted about forty-five minutes and that the jury returned its verdict in less than five minutes, and orders the federal judge to verify whether those facts are accurate.
repere.source: Moore v. Dempsey, 261 U.S. 86 (1923), U.S. Supreme Court, opinion of Justice Holmes

carte.punch: Forty-five minutes of trial, under five minutes of deliberation, five men sentenced to death.
carte.idee: In Arkansas in 1919, five Black men are sentenced to death, according to their petition under pressure from a mob. In 1923, the Supreme Court writes that a trial can be nothing but a mask and that a federal judge must examine the facts.
carte.source_courte: Moore v. Dempsey, U.S. Supreme Court, 1923

quiz.question: Why does the Supreme Court send the case back to a federal judge instead of freeing the five men?
choix: Because the five men had confessed their guilt before the jury
Because it does not rule on their guilt, and wants a judge to verify whether the alleged facts are true
Because the Arkansas Supreme Court had already overturned the trial for a procedural defect
Because federal law forbids the Supreme Court from ruling on a State criminal trial
quiz.explication: Holmes writes that the Court does not have to say whether the men are innocent or guilty, only whether their constitutional rights were respected, and that the facts, taken as true, still have to be established. The five men had not confessed, the Arkansas Supreme Court had upheld the convictions, and the federal court can precisely examine this kind of trial.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What keeps the mob from lynching the five accused before their trial?
choix: The governor of Arkansas pardons the five men as soon as they are charged
Federal soldiers keep the mob out, and it is calmed by the promise of a trial in due form
The Arkansas Supreme Court overturns the trial before it begins
Justice Holmes orders their transfer to a federal prison
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the petition, federal soldiers keep the mob from lynching the accused, and a committee appointed by the governor calms it by promising that the law will take its course; no pardon, reversal or transfer occurs at that point.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who defends the five accused at the November 3, 1919 trial, and how does he prepare their defense?
choix: A court-appointed lawyer, who never meets them before the hearing and calls no witness
A lawyer chosen by the accused, who asks for a change of venue
A lawyer from the NAACP, who challenges several white jurors
No lawyer is present; the judge alone handles their defense
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The opinion notes that their court-appointed lawyer had no prior consultation with them, asked for no postponement or change of venue, challenged no juror and called no witness.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens to the five men after the Supreme Court's 1923 ruling?
choix: The Supreme Court acquits them outright and they are freed in 1923
The federal judge imposes a new prison sentence on them in 1924
The governor commutes their death sentences in 1925, and they leave prison several months later
They stay in prison until they die, no pardon ever granted
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Wikipedia, freedom does not come in 1923: the governor commutes the death sentences on November 11, 1925, and the men leave prison several months later, not through an acquittal by the Court or a new sentence from the federal judge.
